blocks.text: “I declare,” he says, “I solemnly declare this. Until this crime is discovered and punished by the law, I almost feel as if there were a shameful mark upon my name. A gentleman gave a large part of his life to me. He gave the last day of his life to me. He always sat at my table and slept under my roof. That gentleman went from my house to his own, and he was attacked and killed within an hour of leaving my house. I cannot be sure that he was not followed from my house, or watched at my house. He may even have been chosen as a target first because of his connection with my house. That connection may have made people think he had greater wealth and was much more important than his own quiet, modest behaviour showed. I have money, influence, and a high position. If I cannot use them to uncover everyone who committed such a crime, I fail to show my respect for that gentleman's memory. I also fail in my loyalty to a man who was always loyal to me.”

He makes this strong declaration with great emotion and seriousness. As he speaks, he looks round the room as if he were speaking to a large public meeting. Meanwhile, Mr. Bucket looks quickly at him with watchful seriousness. There might almost be a touch of pity in Mr. Bucket's look, if such a bold thought were even possible towards so grand a man.

“Today's funeral ceremony,” continues Sir Leicester, “clearly showed how much the highest people in the land respected my dead friend.” He puts special stress on the word “friend,” because death makes all social ranks equal. “That ceremony, I say, has made the shock of this most horrible and bold crime even worse for me. Even if my own brother had committed it, I would not save him from punishment.”
Mr. Bucket looks very serious. Volumnia says of the dead man that he was the most trustworthy and dearest person!
“You must feel his death as a sad loss to you, miss,” replies Mr. Bucket gently, “no doubt. He was just the sort of man whose death would be a great loss, I'm sure he was.”

In reply, Volumnia lets Mr. Bucket know that her sensitive mind is completely certain it will never recover from this shock as long as she lives. She says that she is upset forever, and that she does not expect at all to smile again. Meanwhile, she folds a letter into a three-cornered shape like a soldier's hat. It is for that impressive and frightening old general at Bath, and it describes her sad state.
“It gives a sudden shock to a sensitive lady,” says Mr. Bucket kindly, “but the feeling will pass in time.”

More than anything, Volumnia wants to know what is being done. Are they going to find that dreadful soldier guilty in court, or whatever the word is? Did he have any helpers in the crime—or whatever the law calls them? And she asks a great many more questions in the same simple, innocent-sounding way.

“Well, you see, miss,” replies Mr. Bucket. He raises his finger in his persuasive way. He is so naturally polite to ladies that he almost calls her “my dear.” “It isn't easy to answer those questions right now. Not right now. I have worked on this case without stopping, Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet,” says Mr. Bucket, bringing Sir Leicester into the conversation because he is so important. “I have worked on it morning, noon, and night. Without a glass or two of sherry, I don't think I could have kept my mind working so hard for so long. I could answer your questions, miss, but my duty does not allow it. Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, will very soon be told everything that has been discovered. And I hope that he may find the result,”—Mr. Bucket looks serious again—“satisfactory to him.”

The weak, tired cousin only hopes that some fellow will be put to death—as an example. He thinks it takes more influence with important people nowadays to get a man hanged than to get a man a job worth ten thousand pounds a year. He has no doubt at all—as an example—that it is much better to hang the wrong fellow than to hang no fellow at all.
